```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)

# draws a table; cells flagged TRUE in `ans` are drawn in the answer color
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && ans[[i]][[j]]
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

# log posterior for 2 positives of 20 with a flat prior, shifted so its maximum is 0
k <- 2
n <- 20
log_post <- function(p) {
  if (p <= 0 || p >= 1) return(-Inf)
  k * log(p) + (n - k) * log(1 - p) - (k * log(0.1) + (n - k) * log(0.9))
}

# Metropolis sampler for p; returns the chain
metropolis <- function(start, step_sd, n_steps) {
  chain <- numeric(n_steps)
  current <- start
  lp_current <- log_post(current)
  n_accept <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(n_steps)) {
    proposal <- current + rnorm(1, 0, step_sd)
    lp_prop <- log_post(proposal)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_prop - lp_current) {
      current <- proposal
      lp_current <- lp_prop
      n_accept <- n_accept + 1
    }
    chain[i] <- current
  }
  attr(chain, "accept_rate") <- n_accept / n_steps
  chain
}

n_steps <- 2000
set.seed(11); chain_a <- metropolis(0.10, 0.08, n_steps)
set.seed(12); chain_b <- metropolis(0.90, 0.02, n_steps)
set.seed(13); chain_c <- metropolis(0.10, 1.5, n_steps)
set.seed(14); chain_d1 <- metropolis(0.02, 0.003, n_steps)
set.seed(15); chain_d2 <- metropolis(0.45, 0.003, n_steps)

burn <- 200
keep_a <- chain_a[-seq_len(burn)]
f2 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 3)

# 1a: six hand steps, using table values rounded to 2 decimals
jumps <- c(-0.08, 0.09, -0.07, -0.17, 0.04, -0.11)
log_u <- c(-0.42, -0.85, -1.61, -0.30, -1.20, -2.05)
lp_r <- function(p) round(log_post(p), 2)
fmt_lp <- function(v) if (is.finite(v)) f2(v) else "-Inf"
current <- 0.30
steps <- vector("list", 6)
for (i in seq_along(jumps)) {
  proposal <- round(current + jumps[i], 2)
  diff <- lp_r(proposal) - lp_r(current)
  accept <- log_u[i] < diff
  steps[[i]] <- list(current = current, proposal = proposal, diff = diff,
                     accept = accept, record = if (accept) proposal else current)
  if (accept) current <- proposal
}
records <- sapply(steps, `[[`, "record")
accepted <- sapply(steps, `[[`, "accept")
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key} (not for student distribution). Answers are in magenta.}

## The scenario

Chytrid fungus (*Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis*, or Bd) has driven
steep declines of the Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog. Field crews
swab frogs' skin and test the swabs for Bd. At one high-elevation pond,
**2 of 20 frogs tested positive**, the same numbers you saw in the
Week 7 *Reading the Interval* WOD. Model the number of positives as
binomial with unknown prevalence $p$, and give $p$ a flat prior,
Beta(1, 1).

The usual Wald interval, $\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$,
gives $0.10 \pm 0.13$, or $-0.03$ to $0.23$. A prevalence below zero
makes no sense. In this Act you run Monday's Metropolis algorithm by
hand, then judge some computer-run chains, to get a better answer.

**What is the prevalence of Bd in this pond, and how uncertain is it?**

Please keep laptops closed for this Act.

## Part 1: Six steps of Metropolis (individual, ~20 min)

The log posterior for these data is
$$\log P(p \mid y) = 2\log p + 18\log(1 - p) + \text{constant}$$
for $0 < p < 1$; outside that range the posterior is 0 (log posterior
$-\infty$). The table lists it on a grid of $p$ values, shifted by a
constant so the largest value is 0.

```{r lookup}
p_grid <- seq(0.01, 0.40, by = 0.01)
lp_grid <- sapply(p_grid, log_post)
cells <- paste0(f2(p_grid), ": ", f2(lp_grid))
lookup <- matrix(cells, nrow = 10)
knitr::kable(lookup, col.names = rep("p: log posterior", 4), align = "cccc")
```

The chain starts at $p = 0.30$. At each step, the proposal is the
current value plus a random **jump**. The second column of random
numbers is $\log u$, where $u$ is a uniform random number between 0 and
1. Both are already drawn for you.

**1a.** Run six steps. For each, find the proposal, look up both log
posteriors, compute the difference (proposal minus current), decide
whether to accept, and write down the value the chain records at that
step.

```{r trace-table, fig.height=3.6}
jump_txt <- c("-0.08", "+0.09", "-0.07", "-0.17", "+0.04", "-0.11")
rows <- lapply(1:6, function(i) {
  s <- steps[[i]]
  c(as.character(i), f2(s$current), jump_txt[i], f2(s$proposal),
    fmt_lp(lp_r(s$current)), fmt_lp(lp_r(s$proposal)),
    if (is.finite(s$diff)) sprintf("%+.2f", s$diff) else "-Inf",
    f2(log_u[i]), if (s$accept) "yes" else "no", f2(s$record))
})
ans_flags <- lapply(1:6, function(i) {
  c(FALSE, i > 1, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
})
blank_table(c("Step", "Current", "Jump", "Proposal", "lp(curr.)", "lp(prop.)",
              "Difference", "log u", "Accept?", "Record"),
            rows, col_widths = c(0.6, 1, 0.9, 1, 1, 1, 1.1, 0.9, 1, 1),
            row_height = 0.52, cex = 0.8, ans = ans_flags)
```

**1b.** A classmate's version of the algorithm writes down only the
accepted proposals and skips the rows where the proposal was rejected.
Write out their chain for your six steps. Why does their chain give the
wrong picture of the posterior?

\ans{Their chain: `r paste(f2(records[accepted]), collapse = ", ")` (vs. the full chain `r paste(f2(records), collapse = ", ")`). Rejections are how the chain piles up time at high-posterior values; dropping the repeats under-weights the peak, so their posterior is too spread out.}

**1c.** The lookup table drops the binomial coefficient, the
denominator of Bayes' rule, and a further constant. Would any of your
accept/reject decisions change if those were put back in? Why or why
not?

\ans{No. Each decision uses only the difference of two log posteriors, and constants cancel in a difference.}

## Part 2: Which chains can you trust? (individual, ~15 min)

A computer ran four Metropolis chains on the same posterior, 2,000
steps each, with different starting values and jump sizes. Chain D is
two chains run side by side from different starting values.

```{r traces, fig.height=6.4}
par(mfrow = c(4, 1), mar = c(3, 4.5, 1.6, 0.5), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
plot_trace <- function(ch, label, col = "black") {
  plot(ch, type = "l", ylim = c(0, 0.9), col = col, xlab = "", ylab = "p",
       main = label, las = 1)
}
plot_trace(chain_a, "Chain A")
plot_trace(chain_b, "Chain B")
plot_trace(chain_c, "Chain C")
plot_trace(chain_d1, "Chain D (two runs)", "steelblue")
lines(chain_d2, col = "darkorange")
mtext("Step", side = 1, line = 2, cex = 0.7)
```

**2a.** For each chain, would you use it to describe the posterior? If
not, what went wrong, and what would you change?

```{r trust-table, fig.height=3}
blank_table(c("Chain", "Use it?", "What went wrong (if anything)?", "What would you change?"),
            list(c("A", "Yes", "Nothing; mixes well", "Nothing"),
                 c("B", "After burn-in", "Started far away (0.90)", "Drop first 150 to 200 steps"),
                 c("C", "No", "Jumps too big; sticky",
                   paste0("Smaller jumps (", round(100 * attr(chain_c, "accept_rate")), "% accepted)")),
                 c("D", "No", "Jumps too small; runs never meet", "Bigger jumps; run longer")),
            col_widths = c(0.5, 0.9, 2.4, 2.3), row_height = 0.65, cex = 0.85,
            ans = rep(list(c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)), 4))
```

**2b.** About how many steps of Chain B would you throw away before
using it, and why?

Steps to discard: \ans{about 150-200}

\ans{It takes that long to move from its start (0.90) into the posterior (first below 0.3 at step `r which(chain_b < 0.3)[1]`).}

**2c.** Here is Chain A after dropping its first `r burn` steps. The
dashed lines mark its 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles.

```{r hist-a, fig.width=5, fig.height=2.4}
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
hist(keep_a, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, main = "", xlab = "Prevalence, p",
     ylab = "Density", col = "grey85", border = "grey60", xlim = c(0, 0.5))
abline(v = quantile(keep_a, c(0.025, 0.975)), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
curve(dbeta(x, 3, 19), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = ans_col)
```

Posterior mean `r f3(mean(keep_a))`; 95% credible interval
`r f3(quantile(keep_a, 0.025))` to `r f3(quantile(keep_a, 0.975))`.

How does this interval differ from the Wald interval ($-0.03$ to
$0.23$), and why? With a flat prior, which named distribution should
this histogram match? (Recall Week 8.)

\ans{It stays above 0 and is lopsided (longer upper tail); the Wald interval is symmetric and crosses 0 because it assumes a parabola-shaped log-likelihood, which fails with few data near the $p = 0$ boundary. The histogram should match Beta(3, 19) (magenta curve; exact interval `r f3(qbeta(0.025, 3, 19))` to `r f3(qbeta(0.975, 3, 19))`).}
